Protests alleging an issue with vote counting or results tabulation must be filed by the end of the day Friday, Nov. 13. Protests dealing with any other irregularity can be filed by noon on Tuesday, Nov. 17.  Any recounts should be completed by the state canvass on Nov. 24, if possible. Still counting votes. Some NC contests have flipped and others remain too close to call. by Sarah Michels, Carolina Public Press November 12, 2026

Still counting votes. Some NC contests have flipped and others remain too close to call.

by Sarah Michels, Carolina Public Press
November 12, 2026

Two years ago, Democrat Charlie Wallin lost his reelection bid to the Watauga County Board of Commissioners by 19 percentage points in a county that went for Kamala Harris by six percentage points. 

This year’s race for the State House couldn’t be more different. Wallin ran against State Rep. Ray Pickett, R-Watauga, to represent the far northwestern corner of North Carolina in the legislature. After Election Day votes came in and some provisional, military and overseas and cured absentee ballots were later counted, Wallin is up by 345 votes, or 0.92 percentage points. 

Wallin wishes he had managed to grab just a few more votes to avoid staying in the recount threshold — up to a 1% difference in votes between the apparent winner and the second-place candidate. 

With only some late-arriving military and overseas mailed ballots to add to the count and potentially, some challenged absentee and early ballots to remove, it’s unlikely that he will lose his lead, but it’s possible. It’s also unlikely that a recount would shift the tally enough for Pickett to win, but not impossible. Wallin said if it did flip, he would call for a recount himself. 

But until Friday’s canvass, and any resulting recounts, election protests or lawsuits, Wallin can’t quite fully celebrate. He is one of several candidates in this holding position. 

After Election Day, counting votes continues 

Most candidates win by a large enough margin on Election night to consider the race over. But every cycle, at least a few contests are very close. In those cases, the attention shifts to ballots counted after Election Day. 

On Election Day, election officials count ballots cast that day, as well as early votes and absentee ballots. 

Between Election Day and the following Tuesday, county election boards will meet at least once to consider provisional ballots. Voters cast provisional ballots when they don’t appear in the official pollbook or did not bring a valid photo ID. Election staff research provisional voters’ eligibility to determine whether their vote should be counted. 

Voters who did not provide a photo ID had until Tuesday at noon to present a valid voter ID to county election officials. If they did, their vote should count. That’s also the deadline for absentee voters whose ballot had something that needed to be fixed to remedy the issue. 

By the end of Tuesday, Nov. 10, county boards counted all these provisional and cured absentee ballots. 

On Friday, Nov. 13, at 11 a.m., every county will conduct a canvass, where official results will be tallied. Between Tuesday and then, a few things could happen to alter the vote totals. 

First, some absentee ballots and early voted ballots could be challenged by voters or the county election boards. This often happens if, say, a voter casts an early vote but then dies before Election Day, or is convicted of a felony in that time frame. Also, mailed military and overseas absentee ballots may continue to arrive. They must be received by county election offices by 5 p.m. on Thursday, Nov. 12, to count. 

Friday morning, county election boards will consider any challenges and add acceptable military and overseas ballots to the count.

Even after the final results are reported, elections could flip. Losing candidates may call for a recount if the difference between their vote total and the leading candidate is less than 1% of the total votes cast in the contest. In elections where voters may choose multiple candidates, the recount threshold is still 1%, but only considering the votes cast for the candidate requesting the recount and the candidate ahead of them. 

Recounts rarely shift more than a few votes. Election protests alleging some irregularity requiring certain ballots to be removed or added are much more likely to change the results. Protests alleging an issue with vote counting or results tabulation must be filed by the end of the day Friday, Nov. 13. Protests dealing with any other irregularity can be filed by noon on Tuesday, Nov. 17. 

Any recounts should be completed by the state canvass on Nov. 24, if possible. If no protests remain pending, the State Board of Elections will officially certify state-level elections on Nov. 30. County-level races will be certified earlier, on Nov. 19. 

What to watch

Heading into Friday’s canvass, several races remain within the recount threshold. 

In some, the candidate currently behind has already conceded. For example, Republican US Rep. Greg Murphy congratulated Democratic challenger Raymond Smith on his win in a social media post Wednesday. 

“I am sure he will serve the next two years with honor and integrity,” Murphy wrote. “I would be remiss if I did not express personal disappointment in not being able to continue what I believe was good and diligent work on behalf of the people of Eastern North Carolina.” 

Murphy was ahead by less than 300 votes, until provisional ballots and cured absentee ballots were counted. Smith gained enough ground to flip the lead, and now leads Murphy by 293 votes. While that is well within the 1% recount threshold, Murphy decided to call it. 

In a pre-election press call, Smith talked about serving alongside Murphy in the state legislature years ago. He said he once tried to work with Murphy on a Medicaid expansion bill, but that Murphy pulled it at the last second. He added that gerrymandering stripped his seat away; he would focus on voting rights if elected to Congress. 

There haven’t been concessions in three other close US House races. In the 7th Congressional District, Democratic challenger Kimberly Hardy is a couple thousand votes behind Republican US Rep. David Rouzer, within the recount threshold.

Hardy’s campaign manager, Jamaal Doran, told Carolina Public Press that they are considering all options. 

Democrat Ashley Bell is also not giving up in the 10th Congressional District, where she lags about 2,500 votes behind Republican US Rep. Pat Harrigan. In a Facebook post, Bell said her campaign would call for a recount if they remain within the 1% recount threshold. 

“While we are in no way alleging fraud, we have been notified of numerous irregularities, mostly having to do with technology issues, and we will exercise our rights under the law to make sure every eligible ballot is property counted,” she wrote. 

On Election Night, Democrat Chuck Hubbard was just 99 votes ahead of Republican US Rep. Virginia Foxx in the 5th Congressional District race. After provisional and cured absentee ballots were added, he extended his lead to 335 votes. 

Foxx called for nonpartisan election observers to be present during the post-Election Day count to “serve as important, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,” she said in a social media post. 

Meanwhile, Hubbard was already in Washington, D.C., at new-member orientation. 

If all Congressional results stay the same, Democrats will have flipped the delegation from a 10-4 split favoring Republicans to a 11-3 split favoring Democrats. 

A handful of races in the state legislature remain too close to call, too. The most important one is State Senate District 24, where Republican State Sen. Danny Earl Britt Jr., R-Robeson, leads Democrat Catina Hamm by 228 votes, or 0.4%. If Britt loses, the State Senate would have 25 Democrats and 25 Republicans, meaning that Democratic Lieutenant Gov. Rachel Hunt could break ties in Democrats’ favor, giving them effective control of that chamber. 

If his win endures, Britt’s seat will be the one seat holding Democrats back from a trifecta, as they now have control of the governor’s office and the State House of Representatives. Britt did not answer a phone call, email or text Wednesday, but he told WRAL he was confident any recounts or ballot challenges wouldn’t change the result. 

Over in the State House, Democrats earned majority control. But a few races still have to finalized. 

The closest is a New Hanover House District 20 contest between Republican Dane Scalise and Democrat Tim Merrick. Neither candidate has served in the legislature before, but both have local government experience. Merrick is leading by just 81 votes. 

Merrick said he’s heard of 14 voter challenges. He thinks it’s unlikely that his race flips, but if it does, he would only call for a recount if he felt like “people’s rightful votes had been eliminated.”

Merrick has already been talking to Democratic legislative leadership. He said he’s excited to join a large freshman class and feels like party leaders are ready to welcome fresh voices.

In Pitt County’s House District 9, Republican State Rep. Tim Reeder isn’t throwing in the towel quite yet after trailing behind Democrat Claire Kempner by 225 votes. 

“The results of the election were not what I had hoped, but they are still very close,” Reeder wrote in a social media post. “There are a number of provisional ballots left to be counted. I will await the results of the final tally after canvasing (sic)  next week. At that time, I will respect the will of the voters.” 

Reeder told Carolina Public Press he was not talking to reporters, but would release a statement on Thursday. 

Guilford County’s House District 62 race could be subject to a recount, if Republican State Rep. John Blust asks for one. He currently sits 262 votes behind Democrat Shelly Headen. 

While the Alamance County House District 63 race is within recount territory, Republican Ryan Moffitt conceded to Democrat Ian Baltutis on Wednesday. 

“Ian is a tireless worker for the causes he believes in, including his vision for our community,” Moffitt wrote in a Facebook post. 

“Before this contest, Ian and I had many occasions to collaborate over the years with nothing but positivity and always in the best interest of our community. I look forward to supporting him and our community in his work as our Representative in Raleigh.” 

Wallin’s win feels fairly secure to him, but Pickett could request a recount or file an election protest. Wallin said he knew the race would be close if he won, considering his district’s makeup. 

“I felt like I could win, and we knew the numbers were there,” he said. “Even early on, there was a path that we thought we could pursue.”

Now he’s thinking ahead to January, when new legislators will take office. He’s hoping to heed the messages he heard on the campaign trail. 

“I've heard over and over and over again, people are upset about their education,” Wallin said. “They've been upset about the voucher system and their county here in Western North Carolina losing money. They're still hurting from Helene. There's issues that crop up every day. There’s some issues that have been neglected, and I think we can address them.”
